text: For hundreds of years, millions of Africans were taken across the Atlantic Ocean and forced into slavery.
Later, Europe took over almost all of Africa, but Ethiopia stayed free after defeating an Italian army at Adwa.
src: Between the 16th and 19th centuries more than twelve million Africans were shipped into slavery across the Atlantic

Europe partitioned Africa / the colonial powers divided almost the whole continent among themselves / by 1914 only Liberia and Ethiopia remained independent / Ethiopia’s victory over an Italian army at Adwa in 1896 made it a symbol of African freedom

text: Pan-Africanism is the idea that Africans, and people whose families came from Africa, share one history and future.
Its first meeting, the Pan-African Conference, was called by Henry Sylvester Williams in London, more than 120 years ago.
src: holds that Africans and people of African descent share a common history and destiny
first met under that name at the London conference of 1900 / The Pan-African Conference met at Westminster Town Hall in London from 23 to 25 July 1900, called by Henry Sylvester Williams

text: Marcus Garvey, a printer from Jamaica, built a large movement that taught pride in being Black.
Its slogan was “Africa for the Africans, at home and abroad”.
src: Marcus Garvey, a Jamaican printer and journalist, was its greatest popular organiser / His Universal Negro Improvement Association preached race pride / grew into a mass movement
the slogan “Africa for the Africans, at home and abroad”

text: The American historian W. E. B. Du Bois was the movement's leading thinker for half a century.
About 80 years ago, a meeting in Manchester demanded that Africa's colonies become independent and rule themselves.
src: W. E. B. Du Bois, the American historian and sociologist / was the movement’s leading intellectual for half a century
1945: The Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester demands independence for Africa

text: Many African countries won independence, and Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana called for one united Africa.
Instead, the new states formed the Organisation of African Unity, at a meeting hosted by Emperor Haile Selassie.
src: As seventeen African states won independence in 1960 / Leaders such as Kwame Nkrumah called for a united Africa
the new states founded the Organisation of African Unity in 1963 instead / at a summit hosted by Emperor Haile Selassie

text: Its colours, red, gold and green, are on the flags of many African countries.
Its ideas still shape the plans of the African Union, and they are heard in the reggae of Bob Marley.
src: the red, gold and green of Ethiopia’s flag, which Ghana adopted in 1957 with a black star at its centre and which many African states have used since

Pan-Africanism remains a living ideal / The African Union’s long-term plan, Agenda 2063, and the continental free trade area, which opened for trading on 1 January 2021, are framed in its language / the reggae of Bob Marley
